title: Confidence Interval
body:
A point estimate is one number and is certainly wrong. A confidence interval is that number with an
honest range attached, and every one of them has the same shape:

$$
\text{estimate} \;\pm\; (\text{critical value}) \times (\text{standard error})
$$

The second term is the **margin of error**. That is the entire topic; the rest is bookkeeping about
which critical value and which standard error.

## The four standard cases

| Estimating | Interval | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ known | $\bar{x} \pm z^*\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ | almost never in practice |
| $\mu$, $\sigma$ unknown | $\bar{x} \pm t^*_{n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ | **the normal case** |
| $p$ | $\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ | $n\hat{p} \geq 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10$ |
| $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ | $(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^*\,\text{SE}_{\text{diff}}$ | two-sample, see [[Hypothesis Testing]] |

Common critical values: $z^* = 1.645$ for 90%, $1.96$ for 95%, $2.576$ for 99%. The $1.96$ is the
[[Normal Distribution]]'s 95% multiplier and it appears everywhere.

## Why $t$ instead of $z$

Because estimating $\sigma$ with $s$ adds a second source of error that the $z$ interval does not
account for. The $t$ distribution is the correction: same bell shape, **fatter tails**, indexed by
$n - 1$ degrees of freedom (the same $n-1$ as in [[Variance]], for the same reason). Fatter tails
mean larger critical values, which means wider intervals, which is the price of not knowing
$\sigma$.

As $n$ grows, $s$ becomes a reliable estimate of $\sigma$ and $t$ converges to $z$. By $n = 30$ the
difference is small, which is where the second rule of thumb attached to that number comes from.
Use $t$ whenever you computed $s$ from the data, which is essentially always.

## What controls the width

$$
\text{width} \propto \frac{z^*\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

- **More confidence, wider interval.** A 99% interval is bigger than a 95% one. Certainty and
  precision trade against each other, and a 100% interval is $(-\infty, \infty)$, which is true and
  useless.
- **More data, narrower interval, at rate $\sqrt{n}$.** Four times the data for half the width.
  See [[Sampling Distribution]].
- **More population variability, wider interval.** Nothing you can do about $\sigma$.

Solving the margin-of-error formula for $n$ is the standard sample-size-planning calculation: fix
the width you want, solve for the $n$ that buys it, and be prepared for the answer.

## What "95% confident" means

> [!warning] The interpretation everyone gets wrong
> **It is a statement about the procedure, not about your interval.** If you repeated the whole
> study many times, 95% of the intervals produced this way would contain $\mu$. The interval in
> front of you either contains it or does not, and there is no probability left in it: $\mu$ is a
> fixed number, not a random one.
>
> So "there is a 95% chance $\mu$ is between 12 and 18" is wrong under the frequentist framework
> this course teaches. The randomness lives in the *interval*, which moves from sample to sample,
> not in $\mu$, which does not. A Bayesian credible interval does mean what people want this to
> mean, and it needs a prior; see [[Bayes Theorem]].

## The connection to testing

A two-sided test at level $\alpha$ and a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval give **the same answer,
always**. Reject $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ exactly when $\mu_0$ falls outside the 95%
interval. They are the same calculation rearranged, and the interval is the more informative of the
two because it shows the effect size and the precision rather than only a verdict. See
[[Hypothesis Testing]] and [[P-VALUES]].
